title: Sylvester's Sequence and the Greedy Egyptian Fraction
content: Sylvester's sequence is defined by $a_0 = 2$ and $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$, producing $2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, 3263443, \dots$ (OEIS A000058). It is exactly the **greedy** sequence for the Egyptian-fraction expansion of $1$: at each stage one subtracts the largest unit fraction $1/a_n$ that keeps the running total strictly below $1$. The file proves the two facts that make the sequence famous — a closed form for the partial reciprocal sums and pairwise coprimality of the terms — and the docstring records that the single algebraic identity $a_{n+1} - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1)$ powers both results.

title: The Recurrence in ℕ
content: The sequence is defined directly on $\mathbb{N}$ by structural recursion, with `syl_zero` and `syl_succ` exposing the base case and the recurrence as rewrite lemmas. Defining `syl : ℕ → ℕ` keeps every term a genuine natural number, which is essential for the divisibility and coprimality results later; the rational-valued reciprocal statements cast into $\mathbb{Q}$ only when needed.

title: Every Term Is at Least 2
content: An induction showing $a_n \ge 2$ for all $n$. The inductive step uses $\mathrm{syl}(k) + 2 \le \mathrm{syl}(k)^2$ (a consequence of $a_k \ge 2$), discharged by `nlinarith`. This bound underpins everything downstream: it guarantees the denominators $a_n$ and $a_n - 1$ are nonzero in $\mathbb{Q}$, and that $a_{n+1} - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1)$ never collapses under $\mathbb{N}$'s truncated subtraction.

title: Lifting the Recurrence to ℤ Avoids Truncated Subtraction
content: In $\mathbb{N}$, subtraction is truncated ($a - b = 0$ when $a < b$), so the raw recurrence $a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1$ is only safe because $a_n \le a_n^2$. `syl_cast_succ` restates the recurrence over $\mathbb{Z}$ via `Nat.cast_sub`, after which ordinary ring arithmetic applies with no side conditions. This is the standard discipline for moving a natural-number recurrence into a field: establish the no-underflow hypothesis once, then compute freely.

title: The Telescoping Per-Term Identity
content:
The algebraic heart of the result: each reciprocal splits as a difference of two consecutive terms of $1/(a_n - 1)$. The proof clears denominators with `field_simp` (using $a_n 
e 0$, $a_n - 1 
e 0$, and $a_{n+1} - 1 
e 0$, all from $a_n \ge 2$) and finishes with `ring`. The identity is precisely the partial-fraction shadow of $a_{n+1} - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1)$.

title: Closed Form for the Partial Reciprocal Sums
content: Summing the telescoping identity collapses the series: $\sum_{k \le n} 1/a_k = 1 - 1/(a_{n+1} - 1)$. The induction's successor step rewrites with `Finset.sum_range_succ`, applies the inductive hypothesis, then cancels via `syl_recip_term` and `ring`. Since $a_{n+1} - 1 \to \infty$ (in fact doubly-exponentially), the infinite reciprocal sum equals exactly $1$ — an explicit Egyptian-fraction representation of unity with an exact error term $1/(a_{n+1}-1)$ at every truncation.

title: The Euclid-Style Product Formula
content: Each term is one more than the product of all earlier terms: $a_{n+1} = \big(\prod_{k \le n} a_k\big) + 1$. The induction uses `Finset.prod_range_succ` and the rewriting $\prod_{k \le m} a_k = a_{m+1} - 1$ together with $a_{m+1} - 1 = a_m(a_m - 1)$. This is the same construction Euclid used to prove the infinitude of primes, where $N = (\prod p_i) + 1$ is coprime to every $p_i$ — here it directly yields coprimality of the sequence.

title: Each Term Divides Any Later Term Minus One
content: A direct corollary of the product formula: for $i \le n$, $a_i \mid a_{n+1} - 1$, since $a_{n+1} - 1$ is exactly the product $\prod_{k \le n} a_k$ and $a_i$ is one of its factors (`Finset.dvd_prod_of_mem`). This is the divisibility bridge that turns the product formula into a statement about common factors.
mathContext: $i \le n \implies a_i \mid a_{n+1} - 1,\quad\text{as } a_{n+1} - 1 = \prod_{k \le n} a_k.$

title: Distinct Terms Are Pairwise Coprime
content: For $i < j$, write $j = i + n + 1$. Then $a_i \mid a_j - 1$, while $\gcd(a_i, a_j)$ divides both $a_j$ and $a_j - 1$, hence divides their difference $1$. So $\gcd(a_i, a_j) = 1$. This is the classic Euclid coprimality argument: a common divisor of $N$ and $N-1$ must divide $1$. Pairwise coprimality gives a second proof that there are infinitely many primes (each $a_n$ contributes a new prime factor).
mathContext: $d \mid a_j \text{ and } d \mid a_j - 1 \implies d \mid 1 \implies \gcd(a_i, a_j) = 1.$
